slides.headline: He spent years measuring how the Indian Ocean is warming. The world's largest Earth science society just gave him its top communications honor.
Roxy Mathew Koll, a climate scientist at the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology, Pune, won the American Geophysical Union's 2026 Climate Communications Prize
slides.body: The AGU is the world's largest Earth and space science society, and the prize - named for Pavel S. Molchanov - is one of only 43 AGU honors awarded globally in 2026. It comes with a $25,000 award and will be presented at AGU's annual meeting in San Francisco this December.

slides.headline: Documented how a warming Indian Ocean is reshaping monsoons, cyclones and marine heatwaves across South Asia.
slides.body: Koll's research tracked the Indian Ocean's warming trend and its downstream effects - shifting monsoon patterns, intensifying cyclones, and more frequent marine heatwaves - work that directly informs how India and its neighbors plan for climate risk. A second Indian scientist, Neelima Satyam of IIT-Indore, was named in the same 2026 AGU cohort for the Devendra Lal Memorial Medal.

slides.eyebrow: Why it matters for Viksit Bharat 2047
slides.headline: Climate risk is now a data problem India is helping solve, not just absorb.
slides.body: A Viksit Bharat by 2047 has to be built with clear eyes about a warming ocean on its doorstep. Recognition like this signals Indian climate science isn't just documenting the problem - it's setting the terms the rest of the world uses to talk about it.
